newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: Slovenia greets signs of NATO membership support.
newsitem.headline: Slovenia greets signs of NATO membership support.

text.p: Slovenian Defence Minister Jelko Kacin on Wednesday greeted signals that the former Yugoslav republic had emerged as the best placed outsider to win NATO membership in the first round of NATO expansion.
"We are extremely satisfied with the process of approaching NATO and we want it to continue like this," Kacin said in a telephone interview with Reuters.

Countries of the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation, which plan to invite Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic to start negotiations on joining the alliance at a summit on July 8 and 9, look keen to send a signal to other former Yugoslav republics of the rewards in store if the Balkans remained peaceful.
"I believe Slovenia would also be invited in July to start negotiations...in order to become a full member in the spring of 1999," Kacin said.
"NATO will not become stronger with Slovenia, but this part of Europe will become significantly more stable," Kacin said.
"This is a clear message to the countries of southeastern Europe how to behave to enjoy full legal status among the most democratic and most economically-developed nations," he added.
Slovenia's government continued to nurture strong diplomatic ties with NATO, which Kacin described as "excellent".
He said 19 defence ministers of NATO members and other European countries had already been scheduled to visit Slovenia in the first half of this year.

Kacin pointed out that Slovenia had established strong defence cooperation agreements with neighbouring Italy and Hungary. He added that Ljubljana also planned to take part in the NATO-led Stabilisation Force (SFOR) in Bosnia, to which it would contribute a helicopter unit later this year.
If Slovenia were accepted into NATO it would be the first ex-Yugoslav republic to join the military alliance.
Slovenian prime-minister designate Janez Drnovsek and his centre-left Liberal Democrats are strong advocates of early NATO membership.
The country's right-wing parties, which are in talks with Drnovsek over the exact shape of the country's next coalition government, also back membership in the alliance.

Drnovsek, who won a vote in parliament 12 days ago giving him a mandate to form the next government, needs the backing of at least two of the three right-wing parties represented in the assembly in order to set up a majority administration.
